question.text: Do prerecorded lecture VODcasts affect lecture attendance of first-yearpre-clinical Graduate Entry to Medicine students?
question.context: There is increasing concern amongst educators that the provision of recorded lectures may reduce student attendance of live lectures. We therefore sought to determine if the provision of prerecorded lecture video podcasts (VODcasts) to first-year Graduate Entry to Medicine (GEM) students, affected attendance at 21 Physiology lectures within three separate pre-clinical modules. Data on lecture attendance, utilization of VODcasts, and whether VODcasts should replace live lectures were drawn from three surveys conducted in academic years 2014-2015 and 2015-2016 on all first-year GEM students in two first-year pre-clinical modules where prerecorded Physiology VODcasts were available for viewing or downloading prior to scheduled live lectures. A total of 191/214 (89%) students responded to the three surveys, with 84.3% of students attending all 21 lectures in the study. Only 4% of students missed more than one lecture in each of the three lecture series, with 79% indicating that VODcasts should not replace lectures.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that 79% of students indicated that VODcasts should not replace live lectures. This suggests that the provision of prerecorded lectures did not significantly reduce attendance at live lectures. The high attendance rate (84.3%) further supports this conclusion.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: 79% of students indicated that VODcasts should not replace lectures.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: A potential differential diagnosis could be that students were using VODcasts to supplement their learning, leading to a decrease in attendance. However, the high attendance rate and the majority of students' preference for live lectures make this less likely. Another differential could be that students were using VODcasts as a substitute for attending lectures altogether, but the data doesn't support this.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The data shows that 84.3% of students attended all lectures, with only 4% missing more than one lecture. This high attendance rate suggests that VODcasts did not significantly reduce live lecture attendance. Additionally, 79% of students indicated that VODcasts should not replace lectures, indicating that most students still value the live lecture experience.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether VODcasts might increase attendance (but data shows no significant increase), whether they might reduce attendance (but data shows minimal reduction), and whether they might have no effect (which the data supports as the most likely scenario)

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that 84.3% of students attended all 21 lectures, and only 4% missed more than one lecture, indicating minimal impact of VODcasts on attendance. Additionally, 79% of students believed VODcasts should not replace live lectures, suggesting they did not substitute for live attendance. This strongly supports that VODcasts did not reduce attendance.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 84.3% of students attended all 21 lectures despite access to VODcasts.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered 'yes' (VODcasts reduce attendance) and 'maybe' (uncertain effect), but ruled them out because attendance rates were high and most students preferred live lectures.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Only 4% of students missed more than one lecture in each of the three lecture series, despite VODcast availability.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible concerns about the impact of VODcasts on attendance (e.g., that they might reduce live attendance), but the data shows no significant decrease in overall lecture attendance, ruling out the possibility that VODcasts have a negative effect. Other differentials (e.g., technological access issues) are not mentioned in the case.
